hypotheses.observation: The current live set is 116 registers/thread against a 128-register residency budget, while extending the row value across the reduction requires 144 registers/thread and causes 22.0 GB/s of local spilling; occupancy falls from 0.50 to 0.0625.
hypotheses.mechanism: Keeping the immutable row input live across the reduction crosses the residency threshold, triggering spills and severe occupancy loss.
hypotheses.transformation: Avoid keeping the row input in registers across the reduction; reload or rematerialize the immutable row values at the later use site.
preconditions: The later use can reread the row input without violating the bitwise-equivalence contract.
The added global-memory traffic and reload latency are lower-cost than the observed local spilling.
The compiler or implementation actually shortens the live range and removes the spill.
hypotheses.expected_effect: Potentially restore register residency and substantially improve occupancy by eliminating or reducing local spills, subject to the cost of rereading the row.
risks: Extra global-memory traffic may become the limiting factor.
The reload may not reduce the compiled live set or may introduce additional latency.
Any changed evaluation or conversion order could violate bitwise equivalence.
unknowns: Whether the row input is cache-resident at the later use site.
Whether the compiler can realize the shorter live range.
The runtime contribution of the current spills versus memory reloads.
required_evidence: Compile-time register count and spill bytes after shortening the live range.
Kernel runtime and achieved occupancy with the reload variant.
Memory-throughput and cache-hit measurements for the later row-input use.
Bitwise comparison against the reference dtype output.

hypotheses.observation: The row is mapped one row per thread block, so the same immutable input is reused within a block before and after reduction, but retaining it through the reduction causes the live-set threshold violation.
hypotheses.mechanism: Block-local staging can preserve reuse while decoupling the row input's lifetime from the reduction's accumulator live set.
hypotheses.transformation: Stage the immutable row input in block-shared storage or another explicitly bounded representation, then access it at both use sites instead of retaining all values in per-thread registers.
preconditions: The required shared-storage footprint and accesses fit the block resource limits.
Synchronization and indexing can preserve the original bitwise computation order.
Shared-memory traffic is cheaper than local spilling for this workload.
hypotheses.expected_effect: May reduce per-thread register pressure and avoid the 144-register spill regime while retaining within-block reuse.
risks: Shared-memory footprint, bank conflicts, synchronization, or reduced block residency may offset the benefit.
The transformation may not preserve bitwise-equivalent evaluation order.
It may add complexity without reducing the compiled register allocation.
unknowns: The row width and shared-memory footprint.
The number and pattern of threads accessing each row element.
Whether shared-memory use would reduce or further constrain occupancy.
required_evidence: Row width and per-block shared-memory requirement.
Compiled register, shared-memory, occupancy, and spill metrics.

hypotheses.observation: The measured post-extension occupancy collapse indicates that preserving the current cross-reduction register lifetime is unsafe for residency, but the facts do not establish whether a separate phase is cheaper than reload or shared staging.
hypotheses.mechanism: Separating pre-reduction and post-reduction uses can end the first phase's register live ranges before the reduction, at the cost of an additional boundary and possible reread.
hypotheses.transformation: Evaluate a two-phase or split-kernel organization that materializes the needed intermediate state and recomputes or rereads the immutable row input after the reduction.
preconditions: The intermediate state can be materialized without exceeding memory or synchronization budgets.
Additional kernel-launch or phase-boundary overhead is amortized by the workload size.
hypotheses.expected_effect: Could prevent the cross-reduction live-set extension and avoid the measured spill/occupancy collapse, but benefit is uncertain until phase overhead and bandwidth are measured.
risks: Extra launch, synchronization, and memory traffic may outweigh spill savings.
Materializing intermediates may create another residency or bandwidth bottleneck.
Bitwise equivalence may be difficult if reassociation or execution order changes.
unknowns: Whether the workload is large enough to amortize the split.
The relative cost of spills versus extra rereads.
required_evidence: Intermediate memory traffic and launch/synchronization overhead.
Register, spill, and occupancy metrics for both phases.
Bitwise comparison with the reference output.
